title: The extinction of the cave bear

parts.label: Part 1
parts.title: The extinction of the cave bear
parts.article:
The extinction of the cave bear
 
(A) Hervé Bocherens, an evolutionary biologist at the University of Tübingen, Germany, says his colleagues find his research methods a little 'crude'. He dissolves 30,000-year-old animal bones in hydrochloric acid, which is strong enough to burn through metal, soaks the bone solution in lye, cooks it at about 200 degrees Fahrenheit and freeze-dries it, until what's left is a speck of powder weighing less than one one-hundredth of an ounce. The method may be harsh, but the yield is precious – the biography of a cave bear as told through its chemical components. Bocherens is at the forefront of research on the bear, a European species that died out 25,000 years ago. People have been excavating cave bear remains for hundreds of years— in the Middle Ages, the massive skulls were attributed to dragons — but the past decade has seen a burst of discoveries about how the bears lived and why they became extinct. An abundance of bones has been found from Spain to Romania in caves where the animals once hibernated. 'Caves are good places to preserve bones, and cave bears had the good sense to die there,' Bocherens says.
 
(B) Along with mammoths, lions and woolly rhinos, cave bears (Ursus spelaeus) were once among Europe's most impressive creatures. Males weighed up to 1,500 pounds, 50 per cent more than the largest modern grizzly bears. Cave bears had wider heads than today's bears, and powerful shoulders and forelimbs. But the relationship between humans and cave bears has been mysterious. Were humans prey for the bears, or predators? Were bears the object of worship or fear?
 
(C) Initially cave bears shared the continent of Europe, more than 100,000 years ago, with Neanderthals, a primitive species of humans. Modern humans arrived in Europe about 40,000 years ago, and were soon aware of the bears. They painted images of the animals on cave walls, and carved their likeness in fragments of mammoth tusk. The walls of France's Chauvet cave are painted with lions, hyenas and bears; dating back 32,000 years, these are perhaps the oldest paintings in the world. The painters weren't the cave's only occupants: the floor is covered with 150 cave bear skeletons, and its soft clay still holds paw prints. Most dramatically, a cave bear skull was perched on a stone slab in the center of one chamber, placed deliberately by some long-gone cave inhabitant. 'There's no way to tell if it was just curiosity that made someone put a skull on the rock, or if it had religious significance,' says Bocherens.
 
(D) Another discovery, hundreds of miles to the east of Chauvet, would shed light on the relationship between cave bears and humans. The Swabian Jura is a limestone plateau in southwestern Germany that is riddled with caves. A steel gate guards the Hohle Fels cave from vandals and curiosity-seekers. Floodlights in the cave's main chamber illuminate the ceiling, vaulted like a cathedral above 5,000 square feet of floor space. Long ago, as shown by the bones and tools that archaeologists have found, cave bears and human beings sought shelter here from winter weather. In 2000, University of Tübingen paleobiologist Susanne Münzel unearthed a bear vertebra with a tiny triangular piece of flint embedded in it. The flint was likely a broken spear point, hard evidence of a successful bear hunt 29,000 years ago. Münzel also found bear bones that had clearly been scraped by stone tools. Evidence for bears being a food source for early humans was shown by cut marks on skulls and leg bones where the flesh had been cut away. Many of the bones were from baby bears, perhaps caught while hibernating.
 
(E) Cave bears disappeared not long after humans spread throughout Europe, and one theory is that hunting led to the bears' extinction. Hervé Bocherens' test tubes may hold the clues. Running his white powder through a mass spectrometer, he identifies different isotopes, or chemical forms, of elements such as carbon and nitrogen that reflect what the bears were eating and how quickly they grew. After studying hundreds of bones from dozens of sites in Europe, Bocherens has found that cave bears ate mainly plants. This would have made bears particularly vulnerable to the last Ice Age, which began around 30,000 years ago. This Ice Age shortened or eliminated growing seasons, and altered the distributions of plant species across Europe. Cave bears began to move from their old territories, according to a DNA analysis of teeth found near the Danube River. The cave bear population there was relatively stable, with the same genetic patterns showing up generation after generation. But about 28,000 years ago, newcomers with different DNA patterns arrived — a possible sign of hungry bears suddenly on the move.
 
(F) But changes in the climate can't be solely to blame for the bears' extinction. According to the latest study, by Erik Trinkaus and his colleagues at the Max Planck Institute, cave bear populations began a long, slow decline 50,000 years ago — well before the climate began to change. The new study supports a different explanation for the cave bears' demise. As Neanderthals, and then a growing population of modern humans moved into the caves of Europe, cave bears had fewer safe places to hibernate. An acute housing shortage may have been the final blow for these magnificent beasts.

questions.question: Bocherens' findings on cave bears involve measuring the length of complete bones.

analyses.content: 不要看到“bones”就默认是在量尺寸，原文的动作是“dissolves... in acid（酸溶）”，这与“measuring length”是互斥的操作。
(Paragraph A) "He dissolves 30,000-year-old animal bones... until what's left is a speck of powder... biography... as told through its chemical components."
题目说Bocherens的研究涉及测量完整骨骼的长度。原文A段明确说他的方法是把骨头“dissolves（溶解）”成粉末做化学分析，溶解了就无法测量长度，且研究重点是化学成分而非物理形态，选 FALSE。

questions.question: Bocherens was the first person to conduct analytical research on cave bears in a laboratory.

analyses.content: 题目说他是“第一个（first person）”在实验室对洞熊进行分析研究的人。原文A段只说他在研究的“forefront（前沿/最前列）”，并未提及是否是史上第一人，选 NOT GIVEN。
“处于前沿（forefront）”意味着领先，但不等于“第一个（first）”，不要过度联想。
(Paragraph A) "Bocherens is at the forefront of research on the bear..."

questions.question: Cave bears have been extinct for 25,000 years.

analyses.content: 题目说洞熊已经灭绝了25,000年。原文A段明确提到这是一个“died out 25,000 years ago（在2万5千年前灭绝）”的欧洲物种，选 TRUE。
数字和关键词“died out/extinct”完全匹配。
(Paragraph A) "...a European species that died out 25,000 years ago."

questions.question: At one time, people thought the excavated remains of bears were those of dragons.

analyses.content: “Attributed to” 在这里意为“被认为是......”，对应题目中的 “thought... were”。
题目说人们曾认为挖掘出的熊遗骸是龙（dragons）的。原文A段提到在中世纪，这些巨大的头骨被“attributed to dragons（归因于龙/认为是龙的）”，选 TRUE。
(Paragraph A) "...in the Middle Ages, the massive skulls were attributed to dragons..."

questions.question: Modern grizzly bears are similar in size to cave bears.

analyses.content: 题目说现代灰熊在体型上与洞熊“相似（similar）”。原文B段明确说洞熊比最大的现代灰熊还要“weighed... 50 per cent more（重50%）”，即大得多，并不相似，选 FALSE。
“50% more” 表示显著差异，直接反驳了 “similar in size”。
(Paragraph B) "Males weighed up to 1,500 pounds, 50 per cent more than the largest modern grizzly bears."

questions.question: Neanderthals understood cave bear behaviour better than modern humans did.

analyses.content: 题目比较尼安德特人和现代人谁更了解洞熊行为。原文C段提到了这两种人都与洞熊共存过，也提到现代人画了壁画，但从未比较两者对洞熊行为的“理解程度（understood... better）”，选 NOT GIVEN。
文中出现了两类人，但没有出现比较级的逻辑关系。

analyses.content: (Paragraph C) "...the floor is covered with 150 cave bear skeletons..."
题目说在洞穴地面发现了超过一百具洞熊的____。原文C段提到地面覆盖着150具“cave bear skeletons（洞熊骨架）”，填 skeletons。
“Over a hundred” 对应原文的 “150”，注意填复数。
题目说一个洞熊的____被发现在洞穴显眼的位置。原文C段提到一个洞熊“skull（头骨）”被放置在洞室中央的石板上，位置非常显眼（prominent），填 skull。
“Prominent position” 对应原文的 “perched on a stone slab in the center”。
(Paragraph C) "...a cave bear skull was perched on a stone slab in the center of one chamber..."
题目说洞穴为熊和人类提供了____。原文D段提到洞熊和人类在这里“sought shelter（寻求庇护/避难所）”以躲避冬季天气，填 shelter。
“Provided... for” 对应原文的 “sought... from”，主客体转换，核心名词不变。
(Paragraph D) "...cave bears and human beings sought shelter here from winter weather."
题目说同位素显示____是洞熊的首选食物。原文E段Bocherens发现洞熊“ate mainly plants（主要吃植物）”，填 plants。
“Preferred food” 对应原文的 “ate mainly”。
(Paragraph E) "...Bocherens has found that cave bears ate mainly plants."
题目说冰河时代改变了____里的植被生长（vegetation growth）。原文E段说冰河时代缩短或消除了“growing seasons（生长季节）”，这正是植被生长的改变，填 seasons。
很多人想填 Europe，但原文 “across Europe” 是修饰植物分布的地点。题目问的是 “growth in ______”，原文是 “shortened... growing seasons”，这里考察的是气候对“生长周期”的改变。
(Paragraph E) "This Ice Age shortened or eliminated growing seasons..."
题目说支持上述解释的证据来自对多瑙河附近洞熊种群____中DNA的研究。原文E段提到根据对“teeth（牙齿）”的DNA分析，填 teeth。
“Study of changes in the DNA in the ______” 直接定位到 “DNA analysis of teeth”。
(Paragraph E) "...according to a DNA analysis of teeth found near the Danube River."
题目说人类扩张可能减少了洞熊____的机会。原文F段末尾说由于人类进入洞穴，洞熊拥有更少的安全地方去“hibernate（冬眠）”，填 hibernate。
“Reduced opportunities... to” 对应原文的 “fewer safe places to...”。
(Paragraph F) "...cave bears had fewer safe places to hibernate."
